- If sentiment is strongly bullish (≥ 0.67) in recent days, model tends to overestimate prices; reduce forecast slope or cap upward momentum.
- If sentiment is strongly bearish (≤ 0.33) or shows sharp negative swings, model often underestimates downside risk; add downward buffer or adjust for volatility clustering.
- After a sharp price spike (e.g., >10% from prior peak), model frequently overcorrects and overshoots; apply a “cool-down” rule to cap forecast growth for 3–5 days.
- When sentiment shifts from bullish to bearish (or vice versa) within 5–7 days, model often fails to adjust quickly; introduce sentiment-weighted smoothing or lag correction.
- If true outcome shows strong mean reversion (e.g., price drops sharply after a peak), model tends to ignore it; apply a “reversion bias” rule to dampen forecasts near historical mean or volatility bands.
- For 30-day forecasts, model often fails to capture short-term sentiment-driven volatility; use sentiment history to adjust forecast variance or add stochastic volatility component.
- If sentiment is neutral or mixed (0.33–0.67), model often underperforms; increase forecast sensitivity to sentiment shifts or use sentiment as a momentum multiplier.
